passages.t: ‘The fool says in his heart’, and God among the righteous
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. Of David” (verse 1). Then comes one of the best-known lines in the Psalms: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” (verse 1). At once the psalm ties that thought to how people live: “They are corrupt; their acts are vile. There is no one who does good” (verse 1).

Next the LORD himself looks down. “The LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God” (verse 2). What he finds is grim: “All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one” (verse 3).

The evildoers “devour my people like bread” (verse 4). But they are not as safe as they think. “There they are, overwhelmed with dread, for God is in the company of the righteous” (verse 5). The poor have a shelter: “the LORD is their shelter” (verse 6).

The psalm ends with a longing: “Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is a wisdom psalm. It teaches, like the book of Proverbs, about two ways of living.

The ‘fool’ here is the Hebrew nabal. It does not mean someone who is not clever. It means someone morally senseless, who lives without regard for God or neighbour. In 1 Samuel 25 a rich, harsh man is named Nabal, and his wife says “he lives up to his name: His name means Fool” (1 Samuel 25:25).

‘In his heart’ matters too. The fool is not arguing in public. He has settled it inside: no one will ever call him to account. So he ‘devours’ the poor as easily as eating a meal. Like the wicked man of Psalm 10, his ‘no God’ is a way of life more than a theory. The note on Psalm 10 says more about this.

The same psalm appears again, with small changes, as Psalm 53. There the name ‘God’ is used where Psalm 14 often has ‘the LORD’.
passages.later:
Paul takes up verses 1 to 3 in his letter to the Romans. He weaves them into a chain of Scripture to show that everyone, Jew and Gentile alike, stands in need of God's mercy: “There is no one righteous, not even one. There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God. All have turned away, they have together become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Romans 3:10-12).

Paul's point is not that the fool is worse than everyone else. It is that, in the end, “Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin” (Romans 3:9). Jesus told of a rich man who planned his life as if God did not count, and God said to him, “You fool!” (Luke 12:20).
passages.hard:
Is this verse an insult aimed at people who do not believe in God? No. The book page answers this at 10:4, and the note on Psalm 10 says it at length. The fool of Psalm 14 is someone who lives as if no one will ever judge, so that he can harm the weak. Many honest unbelievers care deeply about justice, and they are not the target here.

Paul shows the real edge of the psalm. He turns its words on everyone, religious people included. Verse 3 is not about ‘them’. It is about all of us.
passages.asks:
The psalm asks where you live as though God does not see. Most people who believe in God still have rooms of life where they act as if he is not there.

It also gives hope to people who are being ‘devoured’. The poor have a shelter. Pray verse 7 for everyone who waits for God to put things right.
